lessons.name: Analyze passages from A Long Walk to Water : Part 1

content.text: Read the following passage from A Long Walk to Water. In this excerpt, Salva, an eleven-year-old boy, is running away from war and joins a new group of refugees.

textContent.text: The old woman gave Salva a bag of peanuts and a gourd for drinking water. He thanked her and said goodbye. Then he caught up with the group, determined not to lag behind, not to complain, not to be any trouble to anyone. He did not even ask where they were going, for fear that his questions would be unwelcome.
He knew only that they were Dinka and that they were trying to stay away from the war. He had to be content with that.

pieces.text: The days became a never-ending walk. Salva's feet kept time with the thoughts in his head, the same words over and over:

content.text: Where is my family? Where is my family?

textContent.text: Every day he woke and walked with the group, rested at midday, and walked again until dark. They slept on the ground. The terrain changed from scrub to woodland; they walked among stands of stunted trees. There was little to eat: a few fruits here and there, always either unripe or worm-rotten. Salva's peanuts were gone by the end of the third day.
After about a week, they were joined by more people—another group of Dinka and several members of a tribe called the Jur-chol. Men and women, boys and girls, old and young, walking, walking.…
Walking to nowhere.

Salva had never been so hungry. He stumbled along, somehow moving one foot ahead of the other, not noticing the ground he walked on or the forest around him or the light in the sky. Nothing was real except his hunger, once a hollow in his stomach but now a deep buzzing pain in every part of him.

content.text: A Long Journey to Safety

elements.text: Before 2011, Sudan was a large country made up of people with different religions, languages, and tribal affiliations. These differences sparked a civil war in 1983 that forced millions of Sudanese people from their villages.

These refugees walked in groups to seek safety, facing threats such as heat, hunger, and wild animals. The groups were often formed based on tribal affiliation, such as Dinka or Nuer. A large number of the refugees were children separated from their families. A Long Walk to Water, written by Linda Sue Park, is based on the true story of one of these boys, Salva Dut.

imageLabel.text: In 2011, after many years of civil war, South Sudan separated from Sudan and became an independent nation.

content.text: Read the following passage from A Long Walk to Water. In this excerpt, Salva, an eleven-year-old boy, is running away from war and joins a new group of refugees.

textContent.text: The old woman gave Salva a bag of peanuts and a gourd for drinking water. He thanked her and said goodbye. Then he caught up with the group, determined not to lag behind, not to complain, not to be any trouble to anyone. He did not even ask where they were going, for fear that his questions would be unwelcome.
He knew only that they were Dinka and that they were trying to stay away from the war. He had to be content with that.

pieces.text: The days became a never-ending walk. Salva's feet kept time with the thoughts in his head, the same words over and over:

content.text: Where is my family? Where is my family?

textContent.text: Every day he woke and walked with the group, rested at midday, and walked again until dark. They slept on the ground. The terrain changed from scrub to woodland; they walked among stands of stunted trees. There was little to eat: a few fruits here and there, always either unripe or worm-rotten. Salva's peanuts were gone by the end of the third day.
After about a week, they were joined by more people—another group of Dinka and several members of a tribe called the Jur-chol. Men and women, boys and girls, old and young, walking, walking.…
Walking to nowhere.

Salva had never been so hungry. He stumbled along, somehow moving one foot ahead of the other, not noticing the ground he walked on or the forest around him or the light in the sky. Nothing was real except his hunger, once a hollow in his stomach but now a deep buzzing pain in every part of him.
<citation>From Linda Sue Park, A Long Walk to Water. Copyright 2010 by Linda Sue Park</citation>

content.text: Read the following passage from A Long Walk to Water. In this excerpt, Salva, an eleven-year-old refugee, has been separated from his family for months.

textContent.text: Salva's mouth closed and opened again, as if he were a fish. He tried to speak, but no sound came out of his throat. He tried to move, but his feet seemed stuck to the ground.
"Salva!" the man said again, and hurried toward him. When the man was only a few steps away, Salva suddenly found his voice.
"Uncle!" he cried out, and ran into the man's arms. Uncle Jewiir was the younger brother of Salva's father. Salva hadn't seen him in at least two years, because Uncle had been in the army.

content.text: Uncle must know about the war and the fighting! Maybe he will know where my family is!

textContent.text: But these hopes were dashed as soon as Uncle spoke. "Are you alone? Where is your family?" he asked.
Salva hardly knew where to begin his answer. It seemed like years since he had run away from his school and into the bush. But he told his uncle everything as best he could.

As Salva spoke, Uncle nodded or shook his head. His face became very solemn when Salva told him that he had not seen nor heard a single word of his family in all that time. Salva's voice trailed off, and he lowered his head. He was glad to see Uncle again, but it looked as if he might not be much help either.
Uncle was quiet for a moment. Then he patted Salva's shoulder. "Eh, Nephew!" he said in a cheerful voice. "We are together now, so I will look after you!"
<citation>From Linda Sue Park, A Long Walk to Water. Copyright 2010 by Linda Sue Park</citation>

content.text: An Incredible Story

elements.text: In 2004, Linda Sue Park's husband, a journalist, met a man named Salva Dut while writing articles about an organization Dut had started called Water for South Sudan. Dut became friends with Park and her husband, and Park was amazed by Dut's story of his life and hardships as a young refugee during the Second Sudanese Civil War.

Park thought that more people should learn about Salva Dut's incredible story, so she wrote the novel A Long Walk to Water based on Dut's experiences. Part of the novel is about the childhood and young adulthood of Salva Dut, based on the memoir Dut wrote about his experiences and the stories he shared with Park. Another part of the novel is about a fictional girl named Nya and her life in South Sudan in 2008.

textContent.text: The old woman gave Salva a bag of peanuts and a gourd for drinking water. He thanked her and said goodbye. content.text: Where is my family? Where is my family?

textContent.text: Every day he woke and walked with the group, rested at midday, and walked again until dark. They slept on the ground. Salva's peanuts were gone by the end of the third day.

content.text: A Long Journey to Safety

elements.text: Before 2011, Sudan was a large country made up of people with different religions, languages, and tribal affiliations. These differences sparked a civil war in 1983 that forced millions of Sudanese people from their villages.

These refugees walked in groups to seek safety, facing threats such as heat, hunger, and wild animals. The groups were often formed based on tribal affiliation, such as Dinka or Nuer. A large number of the refugees were children separated from their families. A Long Walk to Water, written by Linda Sue Park, is based on the true story of one of these boys, Salva Dut.

content.text: Read the following passage from A Long Walk to Water. In this excerpt, Salva, an eleven-year-old refugee, has been separated from his family for months.

textContent.text: Salva's mouth closed and opened again, as if he were a fish. He tried to speak, but no sound came out of his throat. He tried to move, but his feet seemed stuck to the ground.
"Salva!" the man said again, and hurried toward him. When the man was only a few steps away, Salva suddenly found his voice.
"Uncle!" he cried out, and ran into the man's arms. Uncle Jewiir was the younger brother of Salva's father. Salva hadn't seen him in at least two years, because Uncle had been in the army.

content.text: Uncle must know about the war and the fighting! Maybe he will know where my family is!

textContent.text: But these hopes were dashed as soon as Uncle spoke. "Are you alone? Where is your family?" he asked.
Salva hardly knew where to begin his answer. It seemed like years since he had run away from his school and into the bush. But he told his uncle everything as best he could.

As Salva spoke, Uncle nodded or shook his head. His face became very solemn when Salva told him that he had not seen nor heard a single word of his family in all that time. Salva's voice trailed off, and he lowered his head. He was glad to see Uncle again, but it looked as if he might not be much help either.
Uncle was quiet for a moment. Then he patted Salva's shoulder. "Eh, Nephew!" he said in a cheerful voice. "We are together now, so I will look after you!"

content.text: An Incredible Story

elements.text: In 2004, Linda Sue Park's husband, a journalist, met a man named Salva Dut while writing articles about an organization Dut had started called Water for South Sudan. Dut became friends with Park and her husband, and Park was amazed by Dut's story of his life and hardships as a young refugee during the Second Sudanese Civil War.

Park thought that more people should learn about Salva Dut's incredible story, so she wrote the novel A Long Walk to Water based on Dut's experiences. Part of the novel is about the childhood and young adulthood of Salva Dut, based on the memoir Dut wrote about his experiences and the stories he shared with Park. Another part of the novel is about a fictional girl named Nya and her life in South Sudan in 2008.

textContent.text: The old woman gave Salva a bag of peanuts and a gourd for drinking water. He thanked her and said goodbye. Then he caught up with the group, determined not to lag behind, not to complain, not to be any trouble to anyone. He did not even ask where they were going, for fear that his questions would be unwelcome.
He knew only that they were Dinka and that they were trying to stay away from the war. He had to be content with that.

pieces.text: The days became a never-ending walk. Salva's feet kept time with the thoughts in his head, the same words over and over:

content.text: Where is my family? Where is my family?

textContent.text: Every day he woke and walked with the group, rested at midday, and walked again until dark. They slept on the ground. The terrain changed from scrub to woodland; they walked among stands of stunted trees. There was little to eat: a few fruits here and there, always either unripe or worm-rotten. Salva's peanuts were gone by the end of the third day.

Walking to nowhere.

textContent.text: The old woman gave Salva a bag of peanuts and a gourd for drinking water. He thanked her and said goodbye. pieces.text: The days became a never-ending walk. Salva's feet kept time with the thoughts in his head, the same words over and over:

content.text: Where is my family? Where is my family?

textContent.text: Every day he woke and walked with the group, rested at midday, and walked again until dark. They slept on the ground. The terrain changed from scrub to woodland; they walked among stands of stunted trees. There was little to eat: a few fruits here and there, always either unripe or worm-rotten. Salva's peanuts were gone by the end of the third day.

content.text: A Long Journey to Safety

elements.text: Before 2011, Sudan was a large country made up of people with different religions, languages, and tribal affiliations. These differences sparked a civil war in 1983 that forced millions of Sudanese people from their villages.

These refugees walked in groups to seek safety, facing threats such as heat, hunger, and wild animals. The groups were often formed based on tribal affiliation, such as Dinka or Nuer. A large number of the refugees were children separated from their families. A Long Walk to Water, written by Linda Sue Park, is based on the true story of one of these boys, Salva Dut.

imageLabel.text: In 2011, after many years of civil war, South Sudan separated from Sudan and became an independent nation.
